author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
addressee: A congregation assembled for the feast of Saint Antony
occasion: A festal encomium delivered on the commemoration of Saint Antony, celebrating his memory and urging the hearers to imitate his virtues.
argument: Hesychius opens by declaring that the remembrance of the righteous enlightens the world, and he presents Antony as a citizen of heaven and model of every virtue. He confesses that words cannot match Antony's deeds, and that even Paul would lack time to recount the saints. Antony is then praised through a chain of scriptural figures: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, David, Daniel, John the Baptist, John the Theologian (i.e., John the Evangelist), and Paul. The homily applies to Antony texts from the Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Job, Proverbs, and the work the author attributes to Paul (Hebrews), showing him as the father of monastic communities and a conqueror of the devil and the passions. It closes by exhorting the congregation to imitate Antony's zeal, through the grace of Christ.

outline.move: The homily opens with praise of the memory of the righteous and presents Antony through a series of honorific titles and biblical comparisons.
Hesychius confesses the inadequacy of words to describe Antony's deeds and begins applying scriptural praises to him, especially from the Psalms and Isaiah.

The praise continues with texts from Jeremiah, Job, Proverbs, and the work attributed to Paul (Hebrews), portraying Antony as the father of monastic communities and conqueror of the passions and demons.
The homily concludes by applying further texts from the work attributed to Paul (Hebrews) to Antony's ascetic struggles, exhorting the congregation to imitate him, and ending with a doxology.

cast.name: Antony
cast.who: Saint Antony the Great, the Egyptian desert monk whose feast is being celebrated.

cast.name: Hesychius
cast.who: The author, a priest of Jerusalem, delivering the encomium.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle, quoted as an example of one whose time would fail in recounting the saints; the author attributes the Epistle to the Hebrews to him.

cast.name: David
cast.who: The psalmist, invoked to crown Antony with praise.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.who: The prophet, quoted in praise of Antony.

cast.name: Jeremiah
cast.who: The prophet, quoted as speaking of Antony's sanctification from the womb.

cast.name: Job
cast.who: The righteous man whose story provides a crown of praise for Antony; the author quotes Job 1:1 and adapts a phrase from Job 1:3 allegorically.

cast.name: Solomon
cast.who: The wise king, quoted from Proverbs in praise of Antony.

cast.name: Elijah
cast.who: The prophet whose meekness Antony imitated.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The Lord, invoked to seal the praises and in the closing doxology.

voices.speaker: Hesychius
voices.how_marked: The main voice of the homily, speaking in the first person plural and singular.

voices.speaker: Paul (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'τὰ τοῦ Παύλου εἴπωμεν' and 'φησί', quoting Hebrews 11:32, with the names in the LXX order (Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel) which differs from the order in modern critical editions.

voices.speaker: David (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced as the words of David's lyre, quoting Psalm 111:1-2 LXX.

voices.speaker: Isaiah (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'Λεγέτω περὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ Ἠσαΐας ὁ προφήτης', quoting Isaiah 31:9 LXX.

voices.speaker: Jeremiah (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'τῆς Ἰερεμίου προφητείας τὰ ῥήματα', quoting Jeremiah 1:5.

voices.speaker: Job (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Ἰὼβ ἱστορίας', quoting Job 1:1, with the addition of a phrase from Job 1:3 ('εὐγενὴς τῶν ἀφ' ἡλίου ἀνατολῶν') interpreted allegorically as referring to the 'sun of righteousness'.

voices.speaker: Solomon (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'Σολομών τι περὶ τοῦ δικαίου τούτου καὶ αὐτὸς παροιμιάσασθαι δύναται', quoting Proverbs 20:6 LXX.

voices.speaker: Paul (quoted again)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'Παῦλος δὲ οὐχ οὕτως. Ἀλλὰ τί φησιν;', quoting Hebrews 11:33-35, with Hesychius providing allegorical interpretation of each element.

voices.speaker: Christ (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'ἔτι καὶ νῦν λέγων', quoting Matthew 11:12, with the variant reading βιαστή ἐστι (the text has the reading found in some manuscripts, though the exact form should be verified).

key_terms.sense: The righteous ones, whose memory enlightens and gladdens the world; Antony belongs to this company.
The liturgical commemoration of a saint, here Antony's feast, which brings blessing and illumination.
Virtue in general, of which Antony is called the teacher and model.
Virginity, one of Antony's defining ascetic virtues.
Purity or chastity, paired with virginity as Antony's radiance.
Self-control or continence, the ascetic discipline Antony practiced.
Endurance or steadfastness in ascetic struggle.
The ascetic or monastic way of life, understood as Christian philosophy.
A way of life or conduct, especially the monastic community's manner of living formed by Antony's example.
Spiritual offspring or descendants, the monastic communities throughout Egypt and the world that trace their lineage to Antony.
The demons Antony fought and defeated through his ascetic life.
The devil, Antony's enemy whom he treated as a plaything and trampled underfoot.
Temptations or trials, which Antony counted as gain.
Afflictions or hardships, understood as the road to the kingdom of heaven.
The prize of the heavenly calling toward which Antony pressed in his race.

scripture: The author quotes the Septuagint and follows its book names and Psalm numbering. Citations should be given in modern English form with LXX/Vulgate numbering noted where it differs from the Hebrew, e.g. Psalm 111 LXX = Psalm 112 in Hebrew numbering. The author attributes the Epistle to the Hebrews to Paul, and quotations from it should be cited as Hebrews with a note on the ancient attribution.
uncertain: The precise date of the homily is not stated in the text.
The exact occasion beyond the feast of Saint Antony is not specified.
Whether the homily was delivered in Jerusalem or elsewhere is not stated.
The exact manuscript reading of the Matthew 11:12 quotation (βιαστή ἐστι) should be verified.
